# How to build a vacation rental website from a template: step-by-step guide


by


[Guesty Marketing Team](https://www.guesty.com/blog/author/guesty-marketing-team/)


|


November 9, 2026 Reading time: 7 minutes


Share


Share


You can build a vacation rental website in a weekend. Pick a template route, build five core pages, connect a booking engine that shares one calendar with your OTA listings, test a real booking on your phone, and launch. The template is the easy part. What sits behind it decides whether the site takes bookings or just looks good.


Most template results skip the part that costs you money. A $29 design with a calendar you update by hand double-books you on the first busy weekend. Start with how the site connects to your calendar, and pick the look second.


**TL;DR**


- A template gives you layout and design. It does not give you a booking engine, a synced calendar, or payments
- Choose one of three routes: a design-only template, a WordPress theme with a booking plugin, or a website builder connected to your rental software
- Build five pages: homepage, property page, area guide, policies, and contact/FAQ
- Sync availability in real time with Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo, and Expedia, or expect double bookings
- Treat the property page as your most important template, and use Google’s own landing page rules as the minimum
- Guesty® is vacation rental management software that runs your direct-booking site on the same calendar as your OTA listings, so every channel shows the same open dates


## What a vacation rental website template actually gives you


A template is a pre-built layout. You get page structure, fonts, a color system, image slots, and section blocks. It saves design time. That’s it.


A template does not include:


- A booking engine that checks availability and takes reservations
- A calendar that updates when Airbnb or Vrbo books a night
- Payment processing, deposits, or refunds
- Your policies,[house rules](https://www.guesty.com/blog/how-to-create-effective-house-rules-for-your-vacation-rental/) , or tax setup


Everything on that list is where direct booking sites break.


## Choose your template route before you choose a design


Three routes exist. Each one trades up-front cost against ongoing work.


### Design-only templates


General website builders sell polished layouts. When we checked in October 2026,[Webflow’s vacation rentals gallery](https://webflow.com/templates/search/vacation-rentals) listed paid templates between $29 and $129. They look great, but booking usually means embedding a third-party widget or sending guests to an inquiry form.


### WordPress themes with booking plugins


Theme marketplaces carry dozens of rental themes. In October 2026,[ThemeForest’s vacation rental results](https://themeforest.net/search/vacation%20rental) showed themes and kits from about $15 to $89 before tax and fees, several advertising built-in booking systems and iCal or OTA sync. You own every update: theme, plugin, hosting, security, and backups.


### Website builders connected to your rental software


Here the template sits on top of the same calendar, rates, and reservations you already manage. A booking on Airbnb blocks the dates on your site. A direct booking blocks them on Airbnb. Guesty Websites works this way, with industry-specific templates, drag-and-drop editing, an integrated booking engine and payment gateways, and real-time availability and rate sync through a native API. Already have a site you like? Connect it to the booking engine instead of rebuilding.


Know the difference between iCal and channel manager sync before you commit. An[iCal link](https://www.guesty.com/blog/sync-airbnb-calendar-with-vrbo-calendar/) shares blocked dates between calendars, and each platform pulls updates on its own schedule. It carries no rates or fees. A channel manager connection syncs rates, reservations, and availability together, in real time.


## Template routes compared


Design-only template WordPress theme + booking plugin Builder connected to rental software


Up-front cost $29 to $129 on Webflow (Oct 2026) About $15 to $89 on ThemeForest (Oct 2026), plus hosting Priced as part of a software plan


Availability sync Manual, or a third-party widget iCal or plugin-based, depending on setup Real-time, from the calendar that feeds your OTAs


Double-booking risk High if you update dates by hand Medium, tied to sync timing Lowest, since one calendar feeds every channel


Payments Separate processor or inquiry only Plugin plus gateway setup Built into the booking engine


Who maintains it You You: theme, plugin, hosting, backups The provider runs the booking stack. You own the content


Best fit Inquiry-only sites, brand showcase Hosts who enjoy running WordPress Hosts who want direct bookings without babysitting sync


## How to build your vacation rental website in 7 steps


### Decide whether the site books or only takes inquiries


Boost your short term rentals today


[Get started](https://www.guesty.com/start/)


An inquiry site collects emails and leaves you to confirm each stay by hand, while a booking site takes payment at checkout. Decide now. Want repeat guests to rebook without messaging you first? You need a booking site.


### Register a domain that matches your rental’s name


Use the name guests already know from your listings. Keep it short and skip hyphens. Turn on auto-renew, because a lapsed domain takes your booking page offline.


### Pick a template route and a layout


Choose the route from the table first, then a layout that fits the property. A single-property layout puts one home front and center, with a large gallery and a “Check availability” button that follows the guest down the page.


### Build the five pages every rental site needs


Use this as your content template:


- **Homepage:** One hero photo, a one-line pitch, guest count and bedrooms, the booking widget above the fold, and two or three review snippets
- **Property page:** A full gallery with at least one photo per room, occupancy, bed layout, specific amenities (“EV charger in the driveway,” not “parking”), a live calendar, and a price breakdown showing every fee
- **Area guide:** Drive times to the beach, trailhead, or stadium, three restaurants you actually eat at, and the nearest grocery store and pharmacy
- **Policies:** House rules,[cancellation policy](https://www.guesty.com/blog/guide-to-airbnb-cancellation-policies/) , pet and party rules, check-in and check-out times, and any permit number your city requires you to display
- **Contact and FAQ:** Answers on parking, early check-in, and pets, written before guests have to ask


### Connect booking, calendar, and payments


This step decides whether the site earns anything. Connect the booking engine to the same calendar that feeds Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo, and Expedia. With a[Channel Manager](https://www.guesty.com/features/channel-manager/) , rates, reservations, and availability sync across every connected channel in real time, so a direct booking blocks those dates everywhere at once. Then set up payments: deposit amount, balance due date, and refund rules that match your cancellation policy word for word.


### Write copy guests and search engines can scan


Give each page a title with the property type and location. Add descriptive alt text to every photo. Keep paragraphs to two or three lines, because the site has to read well on a phone. If writing meta descriptions for every page sounds like a lost weekend, Guesty’s[Website optimizer agent](https://www.guesty.com/features/ai-for-short-term-rentals/) drafts SEO and brand-aligned content for direct-booking sites. Edit the draft into your own voice before it goes live.


### Test the full booking on a phone before launch


Book a real night on your own site from your phone. Pay, get the confirmation, cancel, and check the refund. Confirm the dates blocked on Airbnb and Vrbo, then test the reverse.


A guest on a phone picks a weekend the site shows as open. The same dates are already sold on another platform. Two confirmations now exist for one house.


## Your property page is the template that matters most


Google publishes its own rules for where vacation rental links can land. Its[vacation rental referral experience policy](https://support.google.com/hotelprices/answer/10843498?hl=en) says the property details page must show these details without any action beyond scrolling:


- Property name
- Occupancy
- Description
- Photos
- Reviews, if available
- Booking links


Treat that list as your minimum, whether or not you ever appear on Google.


The upside is real. Google’s[free booking links](https://support.google.com/hotelprices/answer/10062327?hl=en) send travelers to book directly on the partner’s website, and Google charges no fees for the referrals or bookings it generates. There’s a catch, though. Google’s[starter guide for property managers](https://support.google.com/hotelprices/answer/12564561?hl=en) says individual homeowners aren’t currently eligible for its vacation rental results, and it points professional property managers to approved connectivity providers. If you rent out your own home, build the site for repeat guests and referrals. Don’t budget on Google traffic.


## Is a free vacation rental website template worth it?


Sometimes. A free template on a general builder works for an inquiry-only site, or for a property where most guests are repeat bookers who message you anyway.


The cost shows up later. Every booking you take by email is a date you block by hand on every OTA. One missed block means a double booking, a cancellation, and a review you’d rather not read. A premium template has the same gap, since a higher price buys a nicer layout on top of the same manual calendar.


The hard part of a vacation rental website is keeping direct bookings, OTA bookings, and payments on one calendar. Run the site on Guesty®[vacation rental management software](https://www.guesty.com/) , whose website builder shares one booking engine and calendar with your Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo, and Expedia listings, and you stop copying dates between dashboards after every direct stay.
